title: Chapter 221 – The Loom of the Road
html:
[Terrace Six – Pebble]

The stair to the Sixth Terrace is longer than it has any right to be, and Pebble climbs it with a dead woman's water skin on his shoulder and a live woman's silence at his back.

He has not spoken since the Orchard. He does not trust his voice. Every time he opens his mouth he sees a small stooped figure in a robe the color of dead grass, standing in a pillar of white light with her arms spread wide, and the words that were going to come out go back down his throat like a tide. So he climbs. He counts the steps, because Master Yue once told him that counting was the cheapest kind of courage, and by the nine hundredth step he has stopped being able to feel his legs.

The stair is a spiral. It winds up and up through a pale mist that smells of wool and lanolin and wet stone. Ahead of him Master Yue climbs with her stone hand trailing along the wall, leaving a thin dry whisper of contact, and behind her goes Master Jian, with his steady hand held loosely at his side as though he were carrying something fragile. Hua walks at the rear with the Lady Veyra. He cannot hear what they say. He has noticed that the Warden has begun to lean, a little, on the hooded woman's arm.

Pebble.

He starts. The voice is Master Jian's, but it has not come through the air. It has come through the mark, the thin gold thread that runs from Hua's palm to the others, the one he has learned to feel as a faint pressure behind the ears.

Sir.

How are you?

I'm all right.

You are not. A pause. Neither am I. It is allowed.

Pebble's throat closes.

She was kind to you, says the voice, more gently. I saw her. When you came up the stair, on the first day, and could not look at the trees. She gave you a cup of tea and did not ask why.

She did.

She would have given you a second one. She would have kept giving you cups of tea until you were forty. The thread hums. That was the kind of Keeper she was. I did not thank her enough. I am telling you so that you will do it sooner than I did.

He wants to answer. He cannot.

He climbs.

---

The mist thins at the thousandth step, and the sound begins.

It is a soft, steady, dry clatter, like a thousand hailstones on a thousand roofs. It rises from the stair ahead, and it is not one sound but many: the thump of a heavy beam, the slide of a shuttle, the rattle of a thousand harnesses lifting and falling, the long breathy sigh of thread paying out through a reed. Pebble has heard something like it before, in the dye-houses of the lower Wall, where the women worked all night to clothe the garrison. He has never heard it like this. It is as vast as the sea.

The stair ends in a door of pale wood, wide as a barn, standing ajar.

Beyond it there is light. Not the gold of the Orchard but a silver-white, cool and even, like moonlight through linen. Pebble steps through the doorway with the others at his heels and stops dead.

He is standing at the edge of a floor that has no end.

It is a vast flat plain of pale boards, polished by a million feet, running away on every side to a horizon of silver mist. And standing on it, in ranks, in rows, in endless regular files that fade into the distance, are looms.

They are enormous. The nearest is ten times his height, a lattice of dark beams and rollers and harness frames, strung from floor to ceiling with threads so fine that they are visible only as a faint bright shimmer in the air. Each is manned. Between the beams, on narrow plank bridges, tiny figures move: men and women and children in plain undyed smocks, passing shuttles hand to hand, tamping the weft with comb-beaters as long as their arms. They do not look up. They do not speak. They work with the unhurried perfection of people who have done the same motion a million times and will do it a million more.

Weavers, says Veyra, very quietly, behind him. Passengers who stayed.

"Stayed?"

They did not climb. They paid the fare, and stopped here, and the Loom took them. She does not sound surprised. Some of them have been at it for two hundred years. They do not age. They do not tire. They are not unhappy. A silence. They are not anything.

Pebble looks at the nearest figure, a girl of perhaps twelve in a pale smock, with a shuttle in her hand and an empty, patient face. Her eyes are open. They do not blink.

He feels the hair rise on his arms.

---

"There is a custom," says a voice, "that guests should be offered tea."

It comes from a point a few paces to his left. Pebble turns. He had thought the floor was empty there; he had thought nothing was there but the silver light and the dark lattice of a nearby loom. But a woman is standing at the end of the nearest plank bridge, one hand resting on the rail, and he cannot think how he missed her.

She is old. She is so old that her age has gone round again into a sort of agelessness, a dry smooth timelessness, like a stone at the bottom of a stream. Her hair is white and falls to her waist. Her skin is the color of oatmeal. She wears a long plain robe of undyed linen, and over it, from shoulder to hip, a sash woven of a thousand colors of thread, so bright and intricate that it hurts to look at. Her eyes are closed. Her face, turned toward them, wears a small, patient smile.

She is blind, Pebble thinks. And then, with a cold lurch: no. She is not.

The closed lids are sewn shut with a single white thread.

"I am Tamsin," says the woman. "I keep the Loom. You are the climbers. You have come from the Orchard, and the Orchard is no more." The smile does not change. "I felt it go. It was a great shaking of the warp. I was sorry."

"You knew her," says Master Jian.

"I knew her four hundred years." Tamsin turns her closed face toward the sound of his voice. "We were neighbors. She grew; I wove. It was a fair division. I do not think she ever forgave me for the tea."

"The tea?"

"I never drank hers." A dry soft laugh. "It tasted of the hours. I told her so. She said that was the point." The pale hands move on the rail. "Come. I will not make you stand. There is a place by the north beam where the light is kinder."

---

The place by the north beam is a low platform of boards with a ring of stools around a small iron stove. On the stove a kettle is ticking. Tamsin pours, by feel, into six cups of plain gray clay. Her hands do not shake. She hands the first to Hua, who takes it with a murmured word of thanks and holds it between both palms, as though it were a living thing.

Pebble drinks. It is a mild herbal brew, faintly sweet, faintly like lavender, and at the first sip something that has been clenched in his chest since the Fifth Terrace loosens, very slightly, like a fist uncurling.

"You will want to know the price," says Tamsin.

"I would," says Jian.

"It is a plain one. I do not like to be clever." The old woman sets down the kettle. "The Loom weaves the Road. Every thread you see is a life, and every life is a passenger, and every passenger is a strand in the cloth that holds the Terraces up. When you pay a fare, you give a year. The Orchard grew it. I weave it. The cloth is stronger for every thread, and the Road more certain, and the Door more firmly shut." The closed face turns. "That is the Founders' great arrangement. I have been part of it for four hundred years."

"And the sitting?"

"Ah." The smile deepens. "You want the second year. You want your seeds to ripen into Souls. It is the thing every climber wants, at this stage. And the Orchard is gone."

"Yes."

"I can give it to you."

Nobody speaks.

"I can give it faster, too," Tamsin says. "Sixty to one. A day in the Loom is two months in the world below. A year here, five years of yours. A pair of years, if you are patient, and your seeds will be Souls." She lifts the kettle. "It is a better bargain than the Orchard. It is also a harder one."

Here it comes, thinks Pebble.

"You will weave your own thread," Tamsin says. "It is the only way. You will sit at a loom, and you will pass the shuttle, and the cloth that comes off it will be yourself. Every year, every month, every day you have lived or will live. All of it, from the first breath to the last." Her voice is mild. "And when you have finished the cloth, you will have seen the end."

"The end of the thread," says Hua.

"The end of the life." Tamsin's smile is almost tender. "A passenger who sees her own end can never again be surprised by it. This is the Loom's gift. And its price."

A silence settles over the platform.

Pebble looks at the stove. He looks at the kettle, and the plain gray cups, and the steam curling up into the silver air. He thinks of the Orchard's golden fruit, the tiny figures walking in their amber, and the way each of them had been so small, and so busy, and so unaware.

"If we don't want to know," he says.

He has not meant to speak aloud. His voice cracks. All the faces turn.

"If we don't want to know the end," he says again. "Is there another way?"

"There is always another way," says Tamsin gently. "You may leave. You may take the stair at the far end of the Terrace, and climb to the Seventh, and sit under whatever tree you find. They will not be as kind. They will take the same price." She tilts her head. "But you will not see the end. You will arrive at it unready."

Master Yue speaks.

"Which is worse?"

"For a fighter?" The old Keeper almost laughs. "I should say unready."

---

They decide it in the end by lot, which is Master Jian's idea.

He does not say so. He simply takes five pebbles from the floor, small gray stones worn smooth by the weavers' sandals, and holds them out in his closed fist: one white, four gray. Whoever draws the white goes first. It is the oldest, simplest, fairest rule, and he says as much, with the faint dry humor that surfaces in him sometimes, when he is very tired.

"I should rather not choose," he says. "I have made too many choices."

Pebble draws last.

He has not wanted to. He stands at the edge of the circle, with his hands behind his back and his chin tucked down, and listens to the others take their turns. Hua draws gray. Master Yue draws gray. The Lady Veyra, standing apart, declines with a lift of her hand: I have seen my end, she says. It is in the key. Master Jian himself draws, with a tired ironic grimace, a gray.

There is one stone left in the palm. It is smooth, and round, and it has been warmed by the heat of his hand.

It is white.

"Ah," says Tamsin.

Pebble looks at it.

"Well, boy," says Master Yue, from somewhere above his left ear. Her voice is gruff. "You wanted to be useful."

He takes the stone.

It is a very small thing, no larger than a quail's egg, and it weighs nothing at all. He closes his fist around it. He does not feel brave. He feels about eleven years old.

"I'll go first," he says.

---

He overhears the other conversation by accident, while they set up the looms.

He has gone to fetch water from a cistern at the edge of the platform, and the Keeper and the Lady Veyra are standing a few paces off, in the shadow of a beam, speaking in the low flat voices of two old women who have known each other too long to bother with courtesy. They do not know he is there. He does not mean to listen. But the water is slow to come, and the cistern is cold under his hands, and the words drift toward him through the silver air like threads.

"You have not asked," Tamsin says.

I do not need to.

"You do. Every one of them does. Even you." The old Keeper's voice is dry. "You want to know whether his thread is still whole."

Is it?

"I cannot say. I have not seen it in six hundred years." A pause. "I wove it myself, you know. The first one. In the days when the looms were new and the Founders were still arguing over the pattern. He sat where the boy is sitting now, with a shuttle in his hand, and he did not stop for a week."

What did he see?

"I did not ask." The sewn eyes turn toward the other woman. "I have thought about that for six centuries, Veyra. It is the single thing I regret. I did not ask him what he saw."

For a long moment, there is no sound but the ticking kettle and the far dry clatter of the looms.

He told me once, says Veyra Thann. On our wedding night. He said he had a gift for seeing the shape of things, and that he had never once seen the end of his own. The cool voice is flat. I thought he meant that he was young.

"Perhaps he did."

Perhaps he did not. The hood tilts. Tamsin. If he saw it. If he saw all of it, the wedding and the child and the door, and chose to go on—

"Then he is a braver man than I took him for."

Or a more foolish one.

"Is there a difference?" says Tamsin, quite gently.

The cistern is full. Pebble stands with the heavy skin in his arms, not breathing, and watches the two women stand together in the long shadow of the beam. Neither of them moves. The old Keeper puts out one dry hand and lays it on the other's sleeve, and the hooded figure does not pull away.

I should like to see him, says Veyra, at last. Once. Before the end.

"You will."

You cannot know that.

"I cannot," says Tamsin. "But I have woven a great many threads. And I have noticed that the ones tied together tend to end together." She smiles, faintly. "It is the only rule I have ever trusted."

Pebble backs away, one careful step at a time, until the beam hides him. Then he carries the water back to the stove, and sets it down, and does not say a word.

---

The loom they give him is the smallest on the Terrace.

It stands at the end of a long row, a squat dark frame no taller than a man, with a single beam and four harnesses and a shuttle of pale ash wood that fits his hand as if it had been carved for it. There is a stool. There is a spool of thread, so fine that it is almost invisible, white as a spider's line. And there is a figure waiting by the beam: a young man, perhaps nineteen, in a plain undyed smock, with a vacant open face and eyes like two glass beads.

"This is Corin," says Tamsin. "He will show you the pattern. He has been weaving for three hundred years. He does not speak."

Corin bows.

He takes the shuttle from Pebble's hand, gently, and passes it through the warp. It runs across the loom with a soft dry rattle. He catches it on the other side, lifts the harness, tamps the weft with the comb. The thread lays down in a thin white line. Another pass. Another. Pebble watches, fascinated and horrified, as the cloth begins to appear: a narrow pale ribbon, no wider than his thumb, growing a finger's-breadth at a time.

On the third pass, a color shows in the weave.

It is brown. A dull, muddy brown. It runs across the white like a stain, and as it lies down Pebble feels something in the back of his skull give a small, soft click.

He sees a house.

A small house, of gray stone, with a thatched roof and a vegetable plot. A woman is hanging washing on a line. A girl of six is sitting on the step with a doll made of rags. It is his sister, he realizes, with a jolt like a falling stair. It is Sun, at six, with her braids coming undone and her face turned up to the sun. And behind her, in the doorway, there is a man with Pebble's own nose and Pebble's own chin, wiping his hands on a rag.

Father, he thinks.

The vision wavers and is gone.

"There," says Tamsin, softly, from behind him. "It begins at the beginning. It always does. The first hours are the easiest. They are the ones you remember best." The old voice is very gentle. "It is the end that is hard."

Pebble swallows.

"Show me," he says.

He sits down on the stool. He takes the shuttle in his right hand. He passes it through the warp, and catches it, and lifts the harness, and the thread lies down, white and brown and green and blue, a narrow ribbon of life growing under his hands.

The years go by.

---

It takes him, he will learn afterward, three hours of the Terrace's time. It takes him, in the weaving, a lifetime.

He sees his mother's hands. He sees the walls of the Wall rise stone by stone in the red dawn. He sees the first breach, and the second, and a day in autumn when the sky turned black and his father did not come home. He sees himself, a boy of nine, standing in the mud outside the granary with a torch in his hand and no one to tell him he was allowed to put it down. He sees Elder Gu die. He sees Master Yue, tall and thin and terrible, coming up the stair of the tower with a cup of tea. He sees the Hall of Ten Thousand Names, and a face he has been looking for in every gallery for a year, asleep behind a bronze lamp in a row of sleepers, with her hair spread out on the pillow like a dark fan.

He weeps. He does not stop weaving.

He sees the Orchard. He sees the going-down of the gold. He sees a hand on his shoulder, a stone hand, and the warmth that does not come through it. He sees the Sixth Terrace and the silver loom and a young man with glass-bead eyes. And then, quite suddenly, with no warning, the cloth runs out of past.

The shuttle crosses the warp.

The thread lies down.

And the vision that rises is not a memory. It is a place he has never been.

It is a high white room, round, with a roof of pale glass and a floor of pale stone. In the center there is a ring of nine seats, and in each seat a figure. He cannot see their faces. The light is too bright. But he can see their hands, laid in their laps, and on each hand a ring of ember light with a gap and nine spokes. He sees himself, kneeling at the edge of the dais, with a bowl of water in his hands. He sees someone he knows lying very still on the floor, in a gray cloak, with a stone hand outstretched.

Master Yue, he thinks.

She is not breathing.

The thread runs on.

It runs past that room, past that body, into a long white dark. Pebble's hands keep moving. He cannot stop them. The shuttle goes across, and across, and across, and the cloth comes off the loom, a white ribbon with a thread of brown in it, a thread of green, a long steady thread of gray. It reaches the length of his arm. It reaches the length of his body. It goes on and on, past the age of forty, of sixty, of ninety, of a hundred and ten—

Until, quite suddenly, it stops.

The shuttle falls from his hand.

He is sitting on a stool at the end of a row of looms, in a silver room, with the finished cloth spooled in his lap and a thread of blood running from his nose. The tears have dried on his cheeks. Corin is gone. Tamsin is standing beside him with her sewn eyes turned toward the cloth, and the smile has left her face.

"Well," she says quietly. "That is a very long one."

He looks down.

The ribbon is not white. It is not gray. It is a deep, rich, living red, bright as a vein, and it runs from the end of his arm to the floor and beyond. He has never in his life seen anything so long.

"It means you live," says Tamsin.

"For how long?"

"Longer than any of us." She lays a dry hand on his shoulder. "Longer than the Door. Longer than the Seam. Whatever you do, boy, whatever you choose, you will be there at the end of it. I do not know what that means. I do not think it is a kindness."

Pebble stares at the red thread.

It lies in his hands like a living thing, warm, and faintly pulsing.

"The room," he says. His voice shakes. "The white room, with the nine seats. Master Yue was lying on the floor."

The old Keeper is silent.

"Is that what I saw?" he says. "Is that the end of hers?"

"I cannot say."

"Is it?"

"It is an end," says Tamsin, very softly. "It is not necessarily the one she will take. A thread is not a sentence. It is a pattern. You may weave around it. You may cut it. You may tie it to another." She draws a long breath. "But I have never seen a thread that did not end in the hour it was shown."

He lifts his head.

Across the platform, by the small iron stove, Master Yue is standing with her stone hand at her side and her right hand resting lightly on the hilt of her sword. She is looking at him. She has been looking at him for some time. Her face is calm, and still, and carved out of something harder than grief.

"Pebble," she says.

"Master."

"What did you see?"

He opens his mouth to lie. He has never lied to her. He has never needed to.

And Yue, who is a hard woman, and a patient one, and who has heard a great many men try to lie in a great many rooms, holds up a hand.

"Don't," she says, quite gently. "Whatever it is. Not yet. Let me weave my own."

She walks to the loom.
